Clarity.justification: The paper is well-structured with clear sections (Abstract, Introduction, Related Work, Method, Results, Discussion, Conclusion). The hypothesis, methods (KS/MMD on PCA-reduced features with fixed thresholds 0.07/0.02/0.005), results (28.57% accuracy), and root cause analysis (18.8× drift variance) are explicitly articulated. Logical flow from hypothesis falsification to implications is coherent.

Novelty.justification: Presents an empirical falsification of fixed-threshold semantic versioning using statistical drift detection across 14 dataset pairs. While negative results on ImageNet-derived thresholds generalizing to NLP/vision are useful, the core approach (drift detection for versioning) builds incrementally on prior work like Rabanser et al. (2019) and González-Cebrián et al. (2024) without introducing fundamentally new techniques.

Soundness.justification: Methods (ResNet-50/BERT feature extraction, PCA to 2 components, KS/MMD with max score, predefined thresholds) are appropriate and match the provided code implementation. Results (confusion matrix, per-dataset scores, metrics) are consistent with experiment logs showing 28.57% accuracy and failure to meet 85%/70%/85% targets. Limitations (literature-derived ground truth, 13/14 NLP datasets, MNIST cross-dataset shift) are transparently documented.

Significance.justification: Addresses the important problem of semantic dataset versioning for reproducibility, as highlighted in the workshop context. The quantitative evidence (below-random accuracy, 75% false negative rate for MAJOR changes, dataset-relative drift) provides actionable insights for future adaptive/performance-based approaches. Impact is meaningful for data repositories but bounded by scope limitations.

strengths: Rigorous negative result with detailed failure analysis and quantitative metrics matching code outputs
Clear documentation of limitations and concrete suggestions for alternatives (adaptive calibration, supervised classification, performance-based ground truth)
weaknesses: Ground truth labels derived from literature rather than measured model performance degradation
Limited dataset coverage (primarily NLP, only 1 vision example representing cross-dataset shift)
